newsitem.title: UK: UK natgas sees retracement from recent highs.
newsitem.headline: UK natgas sees retracement from recent highs.

text.p: UK spot natural gas prices softened in the outer months on Tuesday, traders and brokers said, as the anticipated retracement from recent highs appeared to take effect.
But for prompt, prices were steadier with a large volume of gas traded on the day-ahead market.
One large buyer was dominant on the day-ahead market, picking up at least 560,000 therms at prices between 11.65 pence and 11.75 pence a therm.
"Liverpool Bay must have fallen over," said one trader, while another described the gas field offshore the UK's west coast as "teetering."
There were others also active in the day ahead market, with 855,000 therms reported directly by dealers, and it was all done in a tight range between 11.60 and 11.75 pence a therm.
Further forward prices fluctuated over the day, but still ended lower than on Monday in the third, fourth and first quarters.

One dealer said it was bid at 17.30 pence in the morning against offers at around 17.50 pence. Offers then came down considerably, with trade done at 17.10 pence a therm shortly after lunch, before bids came up again later in the day.
Subsequent deals were done at 17.25 pence a therm, with deals also rumoured - but not confirmed - done at 17.20 pence.
A broker said the falls were a retracement which had been widely expected after prices had risen steeply in the second half of last week and on Monday.

But against the trend of softer prices, the market was surprised by a gas year deal done at St Fergus at 13.30 pence a therm - which one trader said netted back to 13.90 pence, or perhaps even 14.00 pence a therm, at the NBP.
This compared with deals done at the NBP at 13.65 and 13.75 pence a therm for the same period.

The seller of the St Fergus gas, describing himself as "over the moon," added "we're now posting 13.50 and people haven't fallen off their chairs yet." He also said "we think it's got a bit further to run," although the evidence from the NBP suggests levels are now coming off.
While the physical market was busy again, IPE futures clocked up their second consecutive day, and fifth consecutive session, with no trade done at all.

The exchange put a brave face on it, saying that participants were not unduly worried, and that with so few players participating, when there is a busy day on the OTC market it naturally deflects people from futures trade.
Wednesday's temperature is expected to come near the seasonal norm, with Transco forecasting 12.4 Celsius against a seasonal normal 12.7 Celsius.
This translates to consumption of 189 mcm, or 44 percent of peak day demand.
